title: Visual Space Perception and Visually Directed Action
authors: Jack M. Loomis, Naofumi Fujita, José A. Da Silva, Sergio S. Fukusima (1992)
research_question: Do natural environments viewed binocularly from a stationary vantage point lead to veridical perception, and how does this relate to visually directed action?

hypotheses.hypothesis: Subjects perceive egocentric distance correctly and use it for open-loop walking, leading to accurate visually directed action.
Visually directed action involves cognitive correction of misperceived distance or unconscious learning to map distorted perception to accurate action.
Conscious perception of space and control of motoric activity are served by partially or wholly independent visual systems.

measures: Interval matching (psychophysical judgment of perceived equality between frontal and depth intervals)
Blind walking (locomotor estimation of target distance or interval endpoints)
Continuous blind pointing (imaginal updating of target location during locomotion)

findings.antecedent: Egocentric distance of intervals (4m-12m) in visual matching task
findings.consequent: Physical inequality required for depth intervals to appear equal to frontal intervals
findings.quote: the depth intervals had to be made considerably larger than the frontal intervals to appear equal in length, with this physical inequality of equal-appearing intervals increasing with egocentric distance of the intervals (4 m-12 m).

Performance was quite accurate in both motoric tasks, indicating that the distortion in the mapping from physical to visual space evident in the visual matching task does not manifest itself in the visually open-loop motoric tasks.

findings.antecedent: Egocentric distance of intervals (4m, 6m, 8m, 10m, 12m) in Experiment 1 matching task
findings.consequent: Ratio of matched depth interval to frontal interval (perceived equality)
findings.quote: a significant effect of egocentric distance, F(4, 36) = 13.88, p < .001

findings.antecedent: Length of frontal interval (1.0m, 1.5m, 2.0m) in Experiment 1 matching task
findings.consequent: Ratio of matched depth interval to frontal interval (perceived equality)
findings.quote: a significant effect of interval, F(2, 18) = 16.36, p < .001

findings.antecedent: Visually directed walking to a single target (open-loop) in Experiment 1
findings.source: Results section for Experiment 1, Walking Task
findings.quote: The mean signed error was -2 cm (undershoot) and the mean absolute error was 24 cm. The corresponding power function exponent was 1.02, indicating near-linearity of the responses.

findings.consequent: Ratio of matched depth interval to frontal interval (perceived equality)
findings.quote: a significant effect of egocentric distance, F(4, 36) = 5.43, p < .001

findings.consequent: Ratio of matched depth interval to frontal interval (perceived equality)
findings.quote: significant effect of interval, F(2, 18) = 29.37, p < .001

findings.antecedent: Interaction of Egocentric Distance × Interval Length × Adjustment Method in Experiment 2 matching task
findings.consequent: Ratio of matched depth interval to frontal interval (perceived equality)
findings.quote: a significant Distance × Interval × Adjustment interaction, F(8, 72) = 2.09, p = .047.

findings.antecedent: Visually directed walking to a single target (first target in a sequence) in Experiment 2
findings.consequent: Accuracy of walked distance to first target
findings.quote: The corresponding power function exponents were .98 and .96, indicating near-linearity of the responses.

findings.antecedent: Visually directed walking to two targets defining an interval (frontal or sagittal) in Experiment 2
findings.quote: the mean intervals were on the average about 50 cm larger than the corresponding physical intervals, indicating some inaccuracy in the walking response.

findings.antecedent: Visually directed walking to two targets defining frontal vs. sagittal intervals in Experiment 2
findings.consequent: Ratio of walked width response to depth response
findings.quote: it is obvious in Figure 7 that despite the perceptual foreshortening of depth intervals relative to width intervals... walking to two targets does not manifest this anisotropy

findings.antecedent: Continuous blind pointing to a previously viewed target in Experiment 3
findings.quote: It averaged 9.4° for Subjects 1-5 in the no-vision condition and 5.4° in the vision condition.

findings.antecedent: Blind walking past a previously viewed target (100cm, 200cm, 400cm nearest approach paths) in Experiment 3
findings.consequent: Mean pointing direction relative to target azimuth
findings.quote: the mean pointing direction nearly coincides with that of the target for all three paths (nearest approaches of 100, 200, or 400 cm).

limitations: The comparability of interval matching tasks (exocentric interval perception) and walking tasks (absolute position response) may be limited, making direct comparison of results difficult.
The apparent inconsistency between systematic errors in visual space perception and accurate visually directed action suggests limitations in current understanding of how these processes are related.

paper_metadata.title: Acoustic Rendering and Auditory–Visual Cross‐Modal Perception and Interaction
paper_metadata.crossref_title: Acoustic Rendering and Auditory–Visual Cross‐Modal Perception and Interaction
paper_metadata.crossref_abstract: AbstractIn recent years research in the three‐dimensional sound generation field has been primarily focussed upon new applications of spatialized sound. In the computer graphics community the use of such techniques is most commonly found being applied to virtual, immersive environments. However, the field is more varied and diverse than this and other research tackles the problem in a more complete, and computationally expensive manner. Furthermore, the simulation of light and sound wave propagation is still unachievable at a physically accurate spatio‐temporal quality in real time. Although the Human Visual System (HVS) and the Human Auditory System (HAS) are exceptionally sophisticated, they also contain certain perceptional and attentional limitations. Researchers, in fields such as psychology, have been investigating these limitations for several years and have come up with findings which may be exploited in other fields. This paper provides a comprehensive overview of the major techniques for generating spatialized sound and, in addition, discusses perceptual and cross‐modal influences to consider. We also describe current limitations and provide an in‐depth look at the emerging topics in the field.
